Photograph: Marty Melville/Reuters View image in fullscreen The English language bill became law in New Zealand despite ministry of justice advice that there were no concerns about the status of the language. Photograph: Marty Melville/Reuters New Zealand New Zealand legislation making English an official language ridiculed as ‘pathetic’ Passing of bill gives English same status as Māori and sign language but, with it already spoken by 95% of country, critics call it ‘a pointless exercise’ Eva Corlett in Wellington Mon 3 Aug 2026 00.06 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 02.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Legislation recognising English as an official language of New Zealand has been passed by parliament, prompting derision from linguists and legal experts and a now-viral broadside from a Māori MP who called it “pathetic”. The English language bill became law on 30 July giving English, which is spoken by 95% of the country, the same official status as te reo Māori (Māori language) and New Zealand sign language. The bill formed part of a coalition deal between the centre-right National party and the minor populist New Zealand First party, whose leader, Winston Peters, has long opposed affirmative initiatives for Māori. National needed to strike deals with New Zealand First and another minor party, Act, in order to govern. Why is the New Zealand government cutting Māori words from some school books? Read more Ministry of justice officials had recommended that lawmakers should not pass the bill, because there was “no evidence to support concerns about the use or status of English as an official language”. Te reo Māori and New Zealand sign language had become official to protect linguistic minorities, they said. However, the coalition government and the major opposition Labour party voted in favour of the bill, with minor opposition parties the Greens and Te Pāti Māori against. During the debate, Green MP Tamatha Paul said the bill was “a pathetic waste of the responsibility of this house”, in a speech that has generated millions of views online. Paul said the coalition government were “snowflakes” who saw the word Aotearoa – the Māori name for New Zealand – and “shiver in their boots”. Speaking on behalf of New Zealand First during the final reading, MP Casey Costello denied the law was trivial or unnecessary. “This is a practical measure. It aligns the statute book with longstanding practice, and provides a clear statement about the status of English within New Zealand’s official framework,” Costello told the house. Peters, who is also the foreign affairs minister, has previously argued the bill was necessary because the use of Māori in public services was causing confusion. Labour, meanwhile, has previously said it was against the law but had voted in its favour in order to move on from a “needless culture war”. New Zealand coalition votes to make English an official language as critics decry ‘cynical’ bill Read more Dr Sidney Wong, a linguist and post-doctoral fellow at crown research centre Te Pūnaha Matatini, said official language status was given to languages in need of protection and services, but English was not under any threat. “The main reason why this bill was put in place was based on ideology – there was this perception that English was under threat, that it doesn’t have the prestige, and it needs that sort of legislative protection. But it doesn’t need that,” he told the Guardian. Wong said if the government was really interested in protecting English, it would be funding research into the way New Zealanders spoke English, but the law did not address this. “That’s where the money should be going. Not spending time on this 70-word legislation that’s not going to benefit anyone.” Dr Dean Knight, a law professor at Victoria University of Wellington, said the legislation was “a pointless exercise” that made no difference legally or practically as English was already the dominant language. “Folk who got excited by this performative law-making will be disappointed to learn that, despite the dog-whistling and claims from its promoters within parliament, it does not mandate priority to the English language in government communications and elsewhere,” he said. “Like before, Aotearoa New Zealand will continue to have three official languages.” Explore more on these topics New Zealand New Zealand politics Māori Winston Peters Asia Pacific Language news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/27/us-de.text: With just over two months to go before the US's midterm elections, Democrats face a problem that goes beyond the familiar question of how to beat President Donald Trump: they are still arguing over what the Democratic Party should actually stand for.The divide between progressives and moderates has been visible throughout this year’s primary season. But in recent weeks, it has become harder to dismiss as an internal family quarrel.Progressive insurgents have scored a series of significant victories, while establishment Democrats have responded with growing anxiety about whether candidates identified with the left can win in November – particularly in swing districts and Republican-leaning states.The irony is that both camps believe they have learned the same lesson from the agonising 2024 defeat.For progressives, the lesson is that moderation has failed. They argue that Democrats spent too long defending the status quo, speaking in cautious technocratic language and relying on opposition to Trump rather than offering voters a compelling economic alternative.Their answer is a much more aggressive populism: lower healthcare costs, higher wages, stronger unions, action against corporate power and a political system less dependent on wealthy donors.For more moderate centrists, the lesson is almost the opposite. They argue that Democrats cannot afford to frighten voters in competitive states by embracing candidates or rhetoric that Republicans can portray as socialist, anti-business or culturally extreme – in their view, all recipes for disaster.That argument has been given fresh ammunition by the primary results. In Florida, democratic socialist Angie Nixon pulled off a huge surprise victory over moderate Alex Vindman in the Democratic Senate primary.In Michigan, progressive Abdul El-Sayed defeated establishment-backed Haley Stevens. And in California, progressive Aisha Wahab overcame heavy spending from outside groups to win a special congressional election.To progressives, these are not isolated upsets. They are evidence that Democratic voters are rejecting the old party establishment.But there is a crucial distinction between winning a Democratic primary and winning a general election – and that is where the moderates' argument begins.Florida, once the ultimate swing state, is perhaps the clearest test. Nixon's victory energised the Democratic left, but she now faces an extraordinarily difficult general election in a state that has moved decisively toward Republicans in recent years.Her candidacy has already triggered an argument within Florida's Democratic leadership over how closely the party should associate itself with democratic socialism.In an ironic twist, the day Nixon was elected senate candidate in Florida, Democrats in the state also chose a conservative and former Republican, David Jolly, to be their candidate for governor.The question for Democrats is now not simply whether progressive ideas are popular. Many “leftist” economic positions are remarkably popular across the electorate; recent Reuters/Ipsos polls found that two thirds of independents support raising taxes on corporations and billionaires and providing government-provided healthcare coverage for all Americans.Other polls suggest that paid family and medical leave are also remarkably popular across the American political spectrum, as are a raise to a $15 federal minimum wage and putting in place AI regulations to protect workers.The more difficult question is whether voters who support those policies will actually vote for candidates who carry the progressive label.That distinction matters because the Democratic coalition is changing. Recent research suggests that the 2026 Democratic primaries are not necessarily showing a wholesale ideological shift to the left; rather, they reflect a growing appetite for economic populism and dissatisfaction with the party establishment.Democratic voters can still describe themselves as moderate while supporting policies traditionally associated with the progressive wing. At the same time, they appear less receptive to some of the cultural issues associated with the left like transgender rights, racial justice or aggressive climate policies.That creates an unusual political opening – and a strategic headache.The Democrats may have discovered that their most potent message is neither traditional liberalism nor traditional centrism, but an economically populist politics that attacks corporate power while avoiding some of the cultural battles that have alienated swing voters.The problem is that the party has not yet agreed on how to package it. And there is another complication: Trump, who remains the Democrats' most powerful galvanising issue.While the Republicans are already trying to use progressive primary victories to reinforce their argument that the Democratic Party is moving toward “socialism”, pointing to the likes of Nixon and El-Sayed as evidence that the Democratic Party is being captured by its radical left wing, the Democrats have a strong incentive to keep the election focused on Trump's unpopular record rather than on their own internal divisions.That strategy could work. Democratic candidates currently enjoy an advantage on the generic congressional ballot, and economic concerns – particularly affordability – are dominating the political conversation. In other words, Democrats may be able to win despite their ideological argument rather than because they have resolved it.But the deeper question is what happens after November.If Democrats make significant gains in the House, or even retake the Senate, moderates will argue that voters rewarded candidates who concentrated on affordability, competence and opposition to Trump rather than ideological transformation.Progressives will make a very different calculation. They will point to their primary victories and argue that the party's future lies in candidates willing to challenge Democratic orthodoxy and mobilise voters who have become disillusioned with the political establishment.Either way, the midterms are becoming not just an audition for Congress, but a fight to establish the Democratic Party's post-Biden, post-Harris, post-Trump identity.The stakes are particularly high because the next presidential contest is already looming in the background. The candidates and factions that emerge strongest from the 2026 cycle will have enormous influence over the battle for the Democratic nomination in 2028.For now, however, there is a practical imperative: win in November. And that requires two very different Democratic parties to behave as one.The progressives want a party that fights harder. The moderates want a party that frightens voters less. Both believe the other side's approach risks losing the election.And that may be the central paradox of the 2026 midterms: the Democrats' greatest electoral opportunity may be their growing advantage on economic issues and voter dissatisfaction with Trump, while their greatest political vulnerability may be the unresolved argument over what they want to do with that opportunity.Two months before Election Day, the Democratic Party has not settled that argument. The voters may have to settle it for them.

BTC POWER and Summit Charging Build 17-Site, 107-Charger US EV Infrastructure Pipeline BTC POWER and Summit Charging are developing a US fast-charging pipeline spanning 17 sites, 107 chargers and 135 charging ports, with Summit targeting 100 charging locations by 2028. Eight sites in Washington, D.C., Texas and California have secured National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure program awards and will deploy 40 DC fast chargers across 56 ports. Summit is separately developing four self-funded California sites with 42 chargers and 54 ports, while another five sites in New York and Pennsylvania will add 25 chargers and 25 ports. BTC POWER is providing its US Build America, Buy America-compliant charging technology, including 320 kW All-In-One chargers. The companies have worked together on technical specifications, federal compliance and project economics since April 2026 Adani Energy Wins $493 Million Transmission Project to Evacuate 4.5 GW of Renewable Power Adani Energy Solutions has secured a INR 47 billion ($492.6 million) transmission project designed to evacuate up to 4,500 MW of renewable and storage power between Karnataka and Maharashtra. The project will be implemented through Satara Power Transmission and completed within 36 months. Infrastructure includes a new 765/400-kV substation at Satara, a 765-kV double-circuit Kolhapur–Satara transmission line and expansion of the Kolhapur pooling station. The programme will add 562 circuit-km of transmission lines and 9,000 MVA of transformation capacity to Adani’s network. It will also support pumped-storage development around Satara, Pune and the Mumbai Metropolitan Region, strengthening the inter-regional link between India’s western and southern electricity grids. Genex Advances 300 MW Solar + 1.7 GWh Battery Project at Bulli Creek Genex Power has moved forward with the EPC process for its redesigned Bulli Creek solar-storage development in Queensland, advancing one of Australia’s largest planned hybrid renewable projects. The first stage has been reconfigured from the earlier 775 MW standalone solar plan to 300 MW of solar paired with a 425 MW / 1,700 MWh battery energy storage system. Bulli Creek’s wider development rights allow up to roughly 2 GW–2.5 GW of renewable and storage capacity, including potential battery capacity of as much as 600 MW / 2,400 MWh. The project is located southwest of Toowoomba and is owned by J-Power-backed Genex. The redesigned configuration aims to shift solar electricity into higher-value evening periods and reduce exposure to negative daytime power prices. ELESELA Reaches Financial Close on 20 MWh Lithuania Battery Project Lithuanian developer ELESELA has achieved financial close for a 20 MWh standalone battery energy storage project in Klaipėda, moving the development into the construction phase. The financing was arranged on a non-recourse basis with Artea Bank, while ZOE Energy Storage has been selected as turnkey system integrator with responsibility for system performance and long-term reliability. Financial close was reached on July 17, 2026. The project adds new flexible capacity to Lithuania’s electricity market as the Baltic region integrates increasing amounts of wind and solar generation and strengthens its independent power system. Standalone batteries can earn revenue through energy arbitrage, frequency services and other grid-balancing products while reducing renewable curtailment. The financing structure also demonstrates growing lender confidence in merchant and contracted European battery-storage assets.
